∮δQ = ∮δW: net heat added equals net work done when the system returns to its initial state
W = ∫p dV for a quasi-static process, the area under the path on a p-V diagram; p(V₂ − V₁) at constant pressure; zero in a free expansion
Energy of the molecules of a system; a property; for an ideal gas ΔU = mc<sub>v</sub>ΔT

c<sub>n</sub> = c<sub>v</sub>(n − γ)/(n − 1); Q = mc<sub>n</sub>(T₂ − T₁); negative when 1 < n < γ
A machine that would give net work with no energy input, or more work than the heat supplied; forbidden by the first law
η = W<sub>net</sub>/Q<sub>in</sub> = 1 − Q<sub>out</sub>/Q<sub>in</sub> ≤ 1

q = 0, w = 0, ΔKE ≈ 0, so h₁ = h₂; an ideal gas keeps its temperature
m<sub>i</sub> − m<sub>e</sub> = m₂ − m₁ and Q − W + m<sub>i</sub>h<sub>i</sub> − m<sub>e</sub>h<sub>e</sub> = m₂u₂ − m₁u₁

No direction, no quality of energy, allows PMM-2, no equilibrium or reversibility test; the second law fills these gaps

takeaways: For a closed system Q − W = ΔE = ΔU + ΔKE + ΔPE; over a cycle the net heat equals the net work because the system returns to the same state.
Moving boundary work is ∫p dV along a quasi-static path, the area under the p-V curve; a free expansion does no work.
Internal energy belongs to stored mass; enthalpy h = u + pv adds the flow work and belongs to mass crossing a boundary.
For an ideal gas c<sub>p</sub> − c<sub>v</sub> = R and γ = c<sub>p</sub>/c<sub>v</sub>; for air 1.005, 0.718, 0.287 kJ/kg·K and 1.4.
Every pV<sup>n</sup> = C path has W = (p₁V₁ − p₂V₂)/(n − 1), with n = 1 handled by the ln formula; Q follows from Q = ΔU + W.
A PMM-1 would create energy; any claim with W<sub>net</sub> > Q<sub>net</sub> in a cycle is rejected by the first law alone.
The steady flow energy equation is one equation for every device; strike out the terms each device lacks and keep the units in kJ/kg.
When the mass inside a vessel changes, use the unsteady mass and energy balances; an empty insulated tank filled from a line ends at γT<sub>i</sub>.
The first law is a ledger, not a compass: direction, quality and the impossibility of a PMM-2 need the second law.
bank_note: Long answers on the first law usually ask for the first law with its sign convention, work and heat for an isothermal, adiabatic or polytropic process, a steady-flow analysis of a named device (turbine, nozzle, boiler, throttle), and, in the newer syllabi, filling or emptying a vessel. Most syllabi also ask for PMM-1 and the limitations of the first law.

bank.q: State the first law of thermodynamics for a closed system undergoing (a) a process and (b) a complete cycle. Explain the sign convention you use, and show that the two statements are consistent.
outline: Process form Q − W = ΔE = ΔU + ΔKE + ΔPE, with every symbol and unit
Cycle form ∮δQ = ∮δW, because the system returns to its initial state
Sign convention: heat in and work out positive
Summing the process form over the processes of a cycle gives the cycle form
A numerical check
answer: Energy stored and energy in transit. A closed system holds a fixed mass. It stores energy E = U + KE + PE: internal energy U of its molecules, kinetic energy mV²/2 and potential energy mgz of the system as a whole. Energy crosses its boundary only as heat Q (driven by a temperature difference) and work W (a moving boundary, a shaft, an electric current).

answer.text: (a) Process form. For a change from state 1 to state 2:
answer.pre:
Q₁₂ − W₁₂ = E₂ − E₁ = ΔU + ΔKE + ΔPE
for a stationary system:  Q₁₂ − W₁₂ = U₂ − U₁
differential form:        δQ − δW = dU

answer: Q₁₂ is the heat added and W₁₂ the work done by the system, in kJ. δ marks small amounts of path functions; d marks the change of a property.

Sign convention. Heat added to the system is positive and heat rejected negative; work done by the system is positive and work done on it negative. With this convention one equation covers every case. (Chemistry books count work done on the system and write Q + W = ΔU; the physics is the same.)

answer.text: (b) Cycle form. In a cycle the system returns to its initial state, so every property, U included, returns to its starting value:
Consistency. Write the process form for each process of a cycle 1 → 2 → 3 → 1 and add:
answer.pre:
(Q₁₂ − W₁₂) + (Q₂₃ − W₂₃) + (Q₃₁ − W₃₁) = (U₂ − U₁) + (U₃ − U₂) + (U₁ − U₃) = 0
⇒ Q₁₂ + Q₂₃ + Q₃₁ = W₁₂ + W₂₃ + W₃₁

answer: The internal energies cancel in pairs because U is a property, so the sum of the process forms is exactly the cycle form. Historically the order was the reverse: Joule’s paddle-wheel experiments showed the cycle form, and the process form follows from it by taking two different paths between the same states, which proves that Q − W depends only on the end states and so defines the property U.

answer.text: Numerical check. A gas takes 80 kJ of heat and does 30 kJ of work in process 1 → 2, then returns to state 1 with 20 kJ of work done on it.

answer: Q₂₁ comes from Q = ΔU + W = −50 − 20 = −70 kJ. Around the cycle ΣQ = 10 kJ = ΣW, and ΣΔU = 0, as both forms require.

Closing check. On a p-V diagram the net work, 10 kJ, is the area enclosed by the loop, and it equals the net heat. A mistake to avoid: taking W₂₁ = +20 kJ for work done on the gas gives Q₂₁ = −50 + 20 = −30 kJ, wrong by 40 kJ.

bank.q: Define internal energy and enthalpy. Show why the combination U + pV appears whenever mass crosses a boundary, and explain why enthalpy, not internal energy, is used for boilers and turbines.
outline: Internal energy: microscopic energy of a fixed mass, a state property
H = U + pV, h = u + pv, units
Flow work pv: the work done to push a kilogram across the boundary
Hence each kilogram crossing carries h + V²/2 + gz
Numerical example
answer: Internal energy. U is the energy stored in the molecules of a system: their kinetic energy of translation, rotation and vibration, plus the potential energy of the forces between them. It excludes the kinetic and potential energy of the system as a whole. U is a property (fixed by the state), extensive, in kJ; u = U/m in kJ/kg. For an ideal gas u depends on T only and Δu = cvΔT.
Enthalpy. H = U + pV and h = u + pv, in kJ and kJ/kg. Since U, p and V are all properties, so is H.

answer.text: Flow work. Picture a kilogram of fluid about to enter a duct of area A. It occupies volume v and so a length L = v/A of the duct. The fluid behind presses on it with force pA and pushes it the distance L across the inlet:
answer.pre: flow work = force × distance = (pA) × (v/A) = pv   (kJ/kg when p is in kPa and v in m³/kg)

answer: So every kilogram that enters carries its own u plus the work pv done on it by the fluid behind; every kilogram that leaves does pv on the fluid ahead. The energy carried across the boundary per kilogram is therefore u + pv + V²/2 + gz = h + V²/2 + gz.

Why enthalpy for boilers and turbines. These are open systems: water and steam flow through them continuously. In the steady flow energy equation the pv terms of inlet and outlet always appear next to u, so writing h saves a step and removes a source of mistakes. Steam tables list h for this reason. For a boiler with no shaft work and small changes of kinetic energy, q = h₂ − h₁; for an insulated turbine, w = h₁ − h₂.
Where internal energy is still right. For a closed system, such as a gas in a rigid tank, no mass crosses the boundary, there is no flow work, and Q − W = ΔU uses u.

answer.text: Numerical example. Dry saturated steam at 1 MPa has ug = 2582.8 kJ/kg and vg = 0.1944 m³/kg:

answer: So about 7 percent of the energy that this steam carries into a turbine is flow work; using u instead of h would lose 194.4 kJ per kilogram.

answer.text: Ideal-gas check. For 2 kg of air heated at constant pressure from 300 K to 400 K:

answer: Closing check. 143.6 + 57.4 = 201.0 kJ, so ΔH = ΔU + Δ(pV) holds number for number.

bank.q: Explain why c<sub>p</sub> is always greater than c<sub>v</sub> for a gas, and derive c<sub>p</sub> − c<sub>v</sub> = R for an ideal gas.
outline: Definitions of c<sub>v</sub> and c<sub>p</sub>
At constant volume no work is done, so all heat raises U
At constant pressure the gas also does work pΔV
Derivation from h = u + pv and pv = RT
Values for air and the ratio γ; liquids and solids have c<sub>p</sub> ≈ c<sub>v</sub>
answer: Definitions. cv = (∂u/∂T)v, the heat per kg per kelvin at constant volume; cp = (∂h/∂T)p, the heat per kg per kelvin at constant pressure. Units kJ/kg·K.
Constant volume. In a rigid vessel no boundary moves, so W = 0 and the first law gives qv = Δu = cvΔT: all the heat raises the internal energy and so the temperature.

Constant pressure. In a cylinder with a free piston the gas expands as it warms and does work pΔv on the surroundings. The first law gives qp = Δu + pΔv = Δh = cpΔT. For the same ΔT the gas needs the same Δu (for an ideal gas u depends on T alone) plus the work, so qp > qv and cp > cv.

answer.text: Derivation. For 1 kg of ideal gas, start from the definition of enthalpy and the equation of state:
answer.pre:
h = u + pv  and  pv = RT
⇒ h = u + RT
differentiate:  dh = du + R dT
ideal gas:      c<sub>p</sub> dT = c<sub>v</sub> dT + R dT
⇒ c<sub>p</sub> − c<sub>v</sub> = R

answer: R is the gas constant of the gas, R = R<sub>u</sub>/M, with R<sub>u</sub> = 8.314 kJ/kmol·K and M the molar mass. Because u and h of an ideal gas depend on T alone, the relation holds at every temperature, even though c<sub>p</sub> and c<sub>v</sub> themselves rise slowly with T.

answer.text: Ratio and useful forms. With γ = cp/cv:

answer: What the difference means. Warming 2 kg of air by 20 K needs 2 × 0.718 × 20 = 28.72 kJ in a rigid tank but 2 × 1.005 × 20 = 40.20 kJ at constant pressure; the 11.48 kJ difference is exactly the work mRΔT = 2 × 0.287 × 20 = 11.48 kJ done on the piston.
Liquids and solids. They expand very little when heated, so the work term is tiny and cp ≈ cv; one value, “the specific heat”, is quoted (4.18 kJ/kg·K for water).
Closing check. 0.718 + 0.287 = 1.005 kJ/kg·K, and 0.287/0.4 = 0.7175 ≈ 0.718 kJ/kg·K from cv = R/(γ − 1), so the numbers are consistent.

bank.q: Define a perpetual motion machine of the first kind and state why the first law forbids it. Give two devices that people have claimed to be PMM-1 and explain the flaw in each.
outline: Definition in its two forms
Cycle form of the first law: W<sub>net</sub> = Q<sub>net</sub> ≤ Q<sub>in</sub>
Efficiency above 100 percent would need energy to be created
Two claimed devices and where the energy balance fails
answer: Definition. A perpetual motion machine of the first kind (PMM-1) is a device that, running in a cycle, delivers net work with no energy input, or delivers more work than the energy supplied to it. Equivalently: a machine that creates energy.

answer.text: Why the first law forbids it. For any cycle the system returns to its initial state, so ΔU = 0 and

answer: With no heat exchanged (Q<sub>net</sub> = 0), W<sub>net</sub> = 0: no work. And because Q<sub>out</sub> ≥ 0, W<sub>net</sub> ≤ Q<sub>in</sub>, so the efficiency η = W<sub>net</sub>/Q<sub>in</sub> can never exceed 1. A claim of 125 percent would mean 125 kJ of work from 100 kJ of heat, with 25 kJ created. Conversely, the first law can be stated as “a PMM-1 is impossible”.

Device 1: the overbalanced wheel. Weights hinged on the rim of a wheel swing outwards on one side, so that side has a longer lever arm and is claimed to keep the wheel turning for ever. Flaw: over one full turn each weight comes back to the same height, so the gravitational work done on it is zero; fewer weights sit on the long-arm side, so the moments balance. With friction the wheel slows and stops. The cycle balance gives Wnet = 0 − friction losses < 0.

Device 2: a motor driving a generator that powers the motor. The motor turns a generator, whose output is fed back to the motor, with “surplus” output claimed for lighting. Flaw: if the motor draws P watts, the shaft delivers ηP and the generator returns at most ηgηP. With η = ηg = 0.9 the loop returns 0.81P: 19 percent of the power is lost as heat each pass, so the set runs down, let alone powers a lamp.
What PMM-1 is not. A machine with low efficiency is not a PMM-1, and a machine that conserves energy but turns all heat from one reservoir into work is a PMM-2, which the second law forbids.
Closing check. For claim C, 80 − 20 = 60 kW = W, so the first law is satisfied with η = 60/80 = 75 percent; for claim A, 500 − 300 = 200 kW appears from nowhere.

bank.q: One kilogram of air at 500 kPa and 0.2 m³ expands to 100 kPa along pV<sup>1.3</sup> = C. Take R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K and γ = 1.4. Find the final volume, the work done, the change in internal energy and the heat transferred.
outline: V₂ = V₁(p₁/p₂)<sup>1/n</sup>
W = (p₁V₁ − p₂V₂)/(n − 1), kPa × m³ = kJ
T₁ and T₂ from pV = mRT; c<sub>v</sub> = R/(γ − 1); ΔU = mc<sub>v</sub>(T₂ − T₁)
Q = ΔU + W, with its sign
Check with the polytropic specific heat
answer: Data. m = 1 kg, p₁ = 500 kPa, V₁ = 0.2 m³, p₂ = 100 kPa, n = 1.3, R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K, γ = 1.4. The air is a closed system expanding quasi-statically.
W is positive: the air does 103.4 kJ of work on the piston as it expands.

answer.text: Step 5: heat. First law for the closed system:

answer: Q is positive: 25.9 kJ of heat is added even though the air cools by 108 K.

answer.text: Step 6: check with the polytropic specific heat.

answer: Meaning. Because 1 < n < γ, the path lies between the isothermal and the adiabatic. Of the 103.4 kJ of work, 77.6 kJ comes from the air’s internal energy and 25.9 kJ from heat added through the walls. An adiabatic expansion between the same pressures would take all the work from U; an isothermal one would take it all from heat.

answer.text: Placing the path between its neighbours. The same expansion from 500 kPa, 0.2 m³ to 100 kPa along the two limiting paths:

answer: The work and the heat both fall as n rises from 1 to γ, which is the check that the polytropic answer sits where it should. On a p-V sketch the n = 1.3 curve starts at the same point as the other two and ends between them at 100 kPa.

Closing check. Q − W = 25.9 − 103.4 = −77.5 kJ, equal to ΔU = −77.6 kJ within rounding. A mistake to avoid: using γ = 1.4 in the work formula gives (100 − p₂V₂)/0.4 with a different V₂, a different process altogether.

bank.q: Air is compressed from 100 kPa and 0.5 m³ to 500 kPa in a piston-cylinder. Find the work and heat transfer if the compression is isothermal, and compare with the work needed if the same compression were reversible adiabatic between the same two pressures (γ = 1.4). Explain the comparison.
outline: Isothermal: W = p₁V₁ ln(p₁/p₂), negative; ΔU = 0 so Q = W
Adiabatic: V₂ = V₁(p₁/p₂)<sup>1/γ</sup>, W = (p₁V₁ − p₂V₂)/(γ − 1), Q = 0
Compare: to the same pressure the closed adiabatic needs less boundary work because its volume falls less; it ends hotter
To the same volume, or in a steady-flow compressor, the adiabatic needs more
answer: Data. p₁ = 100 kPa, V₁ = 0.5 m³, p₂ = 500 kPa, γ = 1.4; air treated as an ideal gas; W is work done by the gas.

answer.text: Step 1: isothermal. pV = constant, so V₂ = V₁p₁/p₂ = 0.1 m³.

answer: So 80.5 kJ of work is done on the air and 80.5 kJ of heat leaves through the cylinder wall.

answer.pre:
isothermal:  T₂/T₁ = 50/50   = 1
adiabatic:   T₂/T₁ = 79.2/50 = 1.584   (300 K would become 475 K)

answer: Explanation. In the closed cylinder the reversible adiabatic reaches 500 kPa with less boundary work, 73.0 kJ against 80.5 kJ. The air heats up, so its pressure climbs faster and reaches 500 kPa after a smaller volume change (to 0.158 m³ instead of 0.100 m³), and the area under its curve is smaller. The price is a hot gas holding 73.0 kJ more internal energy, not a cool gas at the same volume.

Compared fairly, at the same final volume the adiabatic is steeper all the way and needs 113.0 kJ (it ends at 100 × 5<sup>1.4</sup> = 952 kPa). And in a steady-flow compressor, where the work is −∫v dp rather than ∫p dv, the adiabatic needs γ times its boundary work, 102.2 kJ against 80.5 kJ isothermal. That is why compressors are cooled and why multistage compressors use intercoolers: the closer the path is to isothermal, the less work is spent.

Sketch. On a p-V diagram draw both curves from (0.5 m³, 100 kPa). The adiabatic rises more steeply and meets the 500 kPa line at 0.158 m³; the isothermal meets it further left, at 0.100 m³. Shade the area under each curve: the isothermal area is the larger, 80.5 against 73.0 kJ.

Mistakes that cost marks. Writing “adiabatic compression always needs more work” without saying what is held fixed; using V₂ = 0.1 m³ for the adiabatic case (that is the isothermal volume); and dropping the minus sign, which hides that work is done on the gas.

Closing check. 80.5 kJ isothermal lies between the two adiabatic figures 73.0 kJ (same pressure, closed) and 102.2 kJ (same pressure, flow), and 113.0 kJ to the same volume is the largest because that curve is the steepest over the full volume range.

bank.q: Steam enters a turbine at 3 MPa and 350 °C with a velocity of 60 m/s and leaves at 20 kPa with a velocity of 150 m/s and a dryness fraction of 0.92. The heat loss from the casing is 12 kJ per kg of steam. Find the work output per kg.
outline: Turbine as a steady-flow control volume; changes of height neglected
SFEE with q = −12 kJ/kg
h₁ from the superheated table at 3 MPa, 350 °C; h₂ = h<sub>f</sub> + x h<sub>fg</sub> at 20 kPa
w = (h₁ − h₂) + (V₁² − V₂²)/2000 + q
answer: Assumptions. Steady flow through the turbine; uniform properties at inlet 1 and outlet 2; no change of height; heat lost q = −12 kJ/kg; w is the work delivered.

answer.pre:
h₁ + V₁²/2000 + q = h₂ + V₂²/2000 + w
⇒ w = (h₁ − h₂) + (V₁² − V₂²)/2000 + q

answer: Step 2: inlet enthalpy. At 3 MPa the saturation temperature is about 233.9 °C, so steam at 350 °C is superheated. The superheated steam table gives h₁ = 3116.1 kJ/kg.

answer.text: Step 3: outlet enthalpy. At 20 kPa the saturation table gives Tsat = 60.06 °C, hf = 251.4 kJ/kg and hfg = 2357.5 kJ/kg:

answer: Answer. The turbine delivers about 674 kJ of work per kilogram of steam. For a flow of, say, 10 kg/s that would be 6.74 MW.
Energy check. Per kilogram, energy in = h₁ + V₁²/2000 = 3116.1 + 1.8 = 3117.9 kJ. Energy out = h₂ + V₂²/2000 + w + |q| = 2420.3 + 11.25 + 674.3 + 12 = 3117.85 kJ. The balance closes.

Comments. The kinetic term changes the answer by 9.45 kJ/kg, 1.4 percent; ignoring it is acceptable only if the question says so. Different steam tables differ by about 1 kJ/kg in h, which moves the answer by the same amount. The steam leaves wet (x = 0.92); real turbines limit exit wetness to protect the last blades from erosion.

State of the steam. At inlet the steam is superheated by 350 − 233.9 = 116 °C, so h₁ is read from the superheated table, not from hg. At exit it is a wet mixture at 60.06 °C with 8 percent liquid by mass, so h₂ needs the quality: hg alone would overstate h₂ by 0.08 × 2357.5 = 188.6 kJ/kg.

Mistakes that cost marks. Using V²/2 in J/kg with h in kJ/kg (giving −9450 instead of −9.45); taking hg at 20 kPa (2608.9 kJ/kg) instead of the wet value; adding the heat loss instead of subtracting it, which gives 698.3 kJ/kg.
Closing check. 674.3 + 12 + 9.45 = 695.75 ≈ 695.8 kJ/kg = h₁ − h₂: the enthalpy drop pays for the work, the heat loss and the gain in kinetic energy.

bank.q: Air enters a nozzle at 400 K and 30 m/s and leaves at 300 K. Treat air as an ideal gas with c<sub>p</sub> = 1.005 kJ/kg·K and assume the nozzle is adiabatic with no work transfer. Find the exit velocity.
outline: SFEE with q = 0, w = 0, Δz = 0
h₁ + V₁²/2 = h₂ + V₂²/2
h₁ − h₂ = c<sub>p</sub>(T₁ − T₂); units: V²/2000 in kJ/kg
V₂ = √(V₁² + 2000 c<sub>p</sub>(T₁ − T₂))
answer: Assumptions. Steady flow; adiabatic (q = 0); no shaft (w = 0); no change of height; air an ideal gas with constant cp.

answer.pre:
h₁ + V₁²/2000 = h₂ + V₂²/2000          (all terms in kJ/kg)
⇒ V₂² = V₁² + 2000 (h₁ − h₂)

answer.text: Step 4: energy per kilogram, term by term.

answer: Meaning. The nozzle turns 100.5 kJ/kg of enthalpy into kinetic energy; the temperature falls 100 K and the velocity rises fifteen-fold.

Effect of the inlet velocity. Ignoring V₁ gives √201 000 = 448.3 m/s, only 1 m/s less, because 30 m/s carries just 0.45 kJ/kg. Inlet velocity matters only when it is a sizeable fraction of the exit velocity.

Is the answer physical? The speed of sound in air at the exit temperature is a = √(γRT) = √(1.4 × 287 × 300) = 347.2 m/s, so the exit Mach number is 449.3/347.2 = 1.29. The flow leaves faster than sound, so this nozzle must be convergent-divergent: a purely converging nozzle cannot accelerate a gas beyond Mach 1 at its exit. The energy equation does not know about the shape; it only fixes the speed that the enthalpy drop can buy.

Why the assumptions hold. A nozzle is short and the gas passes through in milliseconds, so there is little time for heat transfer (q ≈ 0). It has no shaft (w = 0), and any height change of a few centimetres is worth g Δz/1000 ≈ 0.0003 kJ/kg, nothing against 100 kJ/kg.

Mistakes that cost marks. Writing V₂² = V₁² + 2(h₁ − h₂) with h in kJ/kg gives V₂ = √(900 + 201) = 33.2 m/s, absurdly low. Using cv instead of cp gives V₂ = √(900 + 143 600) = 380.1 m/s; the flow work belongs in the balance, so cp is right.
Closing check. 449.3²/2000 = 100.94 kJ/kg, which equals 100.5 + 0.45 = 100.95 kJ/kg within rounding.

bank.q: Refrigerant R-134a passes through an expansion valve from saturated liquid at 800 kPa to 200 kPa. Show that the process is isenthalpic and find the exit quality and temperature. State every assumption.
outline: Control volume around the valve: q ≈ 0, w = 0, ΔKE and ΔPE negligible
SFEE gives h₁ = h₂
h₁ = h<sub>f</sub> at 800 kPa; h₂ = h<sub>f</sub> + x h<sub>fg</sub> at 200 kPa
Solve for x; the exit is at the saturation temperature
Throttling is irreversible even though h is constant
answer: Assumptions. (1) Steady flow. (2) The valve is small and the flow fast, so heat transfer is negligible: q = 0. (3) No shaft or moving boundary: w = 0. (4) Inlet and outlet velocities are similar and low, and there is no change of height, so ΔKE and ΔPE are negligible.

answer.text: Step 1: isenthalpic. The SFEE with these terms removed:
answer.pre:
h₁ + V₁²/2000 + gz₁/1000 + q = h₂ + V₂²/2000 + gz₂/1000 + w
⇒ h₁ = h₂

answer: The enthalpy after the valve equals the enthalpy before it. It does not stay constant inside the valve, where the fluid speeds up in the narrow gap; only the end states have equal h.

Step 4: temperature. The exit is a wet mixture at 200 kPa, so its temperature is the saturation temperature, −10.1 °C. The refrigerant falls from 31.3 °C to −10.1 °C without any work or heat transfer.

Meaning. 27.7 percent of the liquid flashes to vapour in the valve; the energy to evaporate it comes from cooling the rest of the stream. Only the 72.3 percent that is still liquid can absorb heat in the evaporator.

Irreversibility. Constant enthalpy does not mean a reversible process. The pressure drop is unresisted (no work is extracted), and entropy rises; a turbine or expander between the same pressures would deliver work and leave a lower enthalpy.

What happens next in a refrigerator. The wet mixture enters the evaporator at −10.1 °C and leaves as saturated vapour at 200 kPa, hg = 38.43 + 206.04 = 244.47 kJ/kg. Each kilogram therefore absorbs q = hg − h₂ = 244.47 − 95.47 = 149.0 kJ from the cold space, the refrigerating effect. Had the liquid reached the evaporator with no flashing (x = 0), it could have absorbed 206.04 kJ; flashing costs 57.0 kJ/kg, which is exactly the 27.7 percent already evaporated in the valve.
About the tables. Different R-134a tables use different reference states, so their h values differ by a constant, but differences such as h₁ − hf2 and hfg, and therefore x, are the same.

bank.q: An insulated rigid tank of 0.4 m³ contains air at 100 kPa and 300 K. It is connected through a valve to a line carrying air at 700 kPa and 300 K. The valve is opened until the tank pressure reaches 700 kPa. Find the final temperature and the mass of air that enters. Take R = 0.287, c<sub>v</sub> = 0.718 and c<sub>p</sub> = 1.005 kJ/kg·K.
outline: Tank as control volume; uniform-state, uniform-flow; Q = 0, W = 0, no exit
Mass balance m<sub>i</sub> = m₂ − m₁; energy balance m<sub>i</sub>h<sub>i</sub> = m₂u₂ − m₁u₁
p₂V = m₂RT₂ gives m₂T₂
Solve for m₂, then T₂
Compare with filling an empty tank (γT<sub>i</sub>)
answer: Model. Control volume: the tank. Uniform-state, uniform-flow: the air inside is uniform at every instant and the line air enters at fixed 700 kPa, 300 K. Insulated and rigid: Q = 0, W = 0. Nothing leaves: me = 0. Kinetic and potential energy neglected. Ideal gas with u = cvT and h = cpT.

answer.pre:
mass:    m<sub>i</sub> = m₂ − m₁
energy:  m<sub>i</sub> h<sub>i</sub> = m₂u₂ − m₁u₁
⇒ (m₂ − m₁) c<sub>p</sub>T<sub>i</sub> = c<sub>v</sub>(m₂T₂ − m₁T₁)

m₁ = p₁V/(RT₁) = 100 × 0.4/(0.287 × 300) = 40/86.1 = 0.4646 kg
m₁T₁ = p₁V/R = 40/0.287  = 139.4 kg·K
m₂T₂ = p₂V/R = 280/0.287 = 975.6 kg·K   (known, though m₂ and T₂ are not)

answer: Energy check. Energy brought in: mihi = 1.991 × 301.5 = 600.3 kJ. Gain of internal energy: m₂u₂ − m₁u₁ = 2.456 × 0.718 × 397.2 − 0.4646 × 0.718 × 300 = 700.4 − 100.1 = 600.3 kJ. The balance closes.

Why the tank heats. Each kilogram of line air brings u = 215.4 kJ plus flow work pv = RTi = 86.1 kJ. The flow work becomes internal energy inside the closed tank. An empty tank would end at γTi = 1.4 × 300 = 420 K; here the 0.465 kg already present starts at 300 K and pulls the mixture down to 397.2 K.

Afterwards. If the tank later cools to room temperature with the valve shut, its pressure falls to p = m₂RT/V = 2.456 × 0.287 × 300/0.4 = 528.7 kPa. To store 700 kPa at room temperature the tank must be topped up again after it cools.
Check against the empty-tank result. Put m₁ = 0 in Step 1: m₂cpTi = cvm₂T₂, so T₂ = (cp/cv)Ti = 1.3997 × 300 = 419.9 K. The general equation reduces to the special case, as it should.

Mistakes that cost marks. Using ui = cvTi for the entering air (that drops the flow work and gives T₂ = 300 K); assuming T₂ = γTi = 420 K although the tank is not empty; and using the steady flow energy equation, which has no term for the energy stored in the tank.
Closing check. 397.2 K lies between Ti = 300 K and γTi = 420 K, as it must for a tank that starts partly filled at the line temperature.

bank.q: A closed system is proposed to follow a cycle in which the net work output is 200 kJ while the net heat supplied is 150 kJ. Using the first law, examine the claim and state what you must check before rejecting it.
outline: For a cycle ΔU = 0, so ∮δQ = ∮δW
The claim has ∮δW > ∮δQ by 50 kJ
Checks: is it really a cycle; are all heat and work terms counted; same units and basis
Conclusion: a PMM-1

answer.text: Step 1: the law for a cycle. The system returns to its initial state, so ΔU = 0 and

answer.pre:
Q<sub>net</sub> = 150 kJ,   W<sub>net</sub> = 200 kJ
Q<sub>net</sub> − W<sub>net</sub> = −50 kJ ≠ 0

answer: Per cycle the system would give out 50 kJ more energy than it receives. Since it ends each cycle in its starting state, with the same stored energy, the 50 kJ would have to be created. Equivalently, its efficiency based on net heat would be 200/150 = 133 percent.
Step 3: what to check before rejecting it.

answer.text: The checks an examiner expects, each with what it would change:

head: Check
Why it matters
rows: Does the system really return to its initial state?
If not, ΔU ≠ 0 and the process form Q − W = ΔU applies: 150 − 200 = −50 kJ would just mean U falls by 50 kJ, possible for one pass but not repeatable.
Electrical work in, a hidden fuel, a battery or a spring that unwinds would supply the missing 50 kJ.
If 150 kJ is the heat supplied and some is also rejected, the shortfall is larger than 50 kJ.
kJ per cycle against kW, or per kg against per cycle, can make a sound claim look wrong.
Work done on the system counted as output, or heat rejected counted as input, can produce the mismatch.

answer: Step 4: conclusion. If the system does run in a cycle and every transfer is counted, the claim violates the first law and describes a perpetual motion machine of the first kind. No choice of bearings, materials or tuning can fix it, because the shortfall is not a loss to be reduced but energy that does not exist.

What a legal version looks like. With 200 kJ of work per cycle the machine must receive at least 200 kJ of net heat. A real engine also rejects heat: at 40 percent efficiency it would take in 500 kJ and reject 300 kJ, and Qnet = 500 − 300 = 200 kJ = Wnet.

Why the process form does not rescue it. If someone argues that the 50 kJ comes from the system’s internal energy, the device is no longer running in a cycle: after one pass U is 50 kJ lower, after ten passes 500 kJ lower, and it must stop when its stored energy runs out. A machine that must be recharged is a store being emptied, not an engine.
Closing check. 500 − 300 − 200 = 0 for the legal engine, against 150 − 200 = −50 kJ for the claim.

bank.q: Air at 800 kPa occupying 0.1 m³ expands to 100 kPa (a) isothermally and (b) reversibly and adiabatically (γ = 1.4). Compare the work produced, explain which path gives more work, and say where the energy for the work comes from in each case.
outline: Isothermal: W = p₁V₁ ln(p₁/p₂); ΔU = 0, Q = W
Adiabatic: V₂ = V₁(p₁/p₂)<sup>1/γ</sup>, W = (p₁V₁ − p₂V₂)/(γ − 1), Q = 0, W = −ΔU
p-V comparison: the isothermal lies above the adiabatic in expansion
The isothermal work is paid by heat from outside; the adiabatic work by the gas’s internal energy
answer: Data. p₁ = 800 kPa, V₁ = 0.1 m³, so p₁V₁ = 80 kJ; p₂ = 100 kPa; γ = 1.4; ideal gas, closed system, quasi-static.

Which gives more work, and why. The isothermal gives 166.4 kJ, nearly twice the adiabatic 89.6 kJ. On a p-V diagram both curves start at the same point, but in expansion the adiabatic p = C/Vγ falls faster than the isothermal p = C/V: as the gas does work adiabatically it cools, so its pressure drops for two reasons, volume and temperature. At every volume beyond V₁ the adiabatic pressure is lower, and it reaches 100 kPa at only 0.442 m³ instead of 0.800 m³. The area under the isothermal curve is therefore larger.

Where the energy comes from. Isothermal: U cannot change (T is fixed), so every kilojoule of work must enter as heat from a reservoir, Q = 166.4 kJ. Adiabatic: no heat enters, so the work is paid entirely from the gas’s own internal energy, ΔU = −89.6 kJ, and the gas cools to 55.2 percent of its absolute starting temperature (from 600 K to 331 K, for example).

Evaluation. More work from the isothermal path is not free energy: it needs a heat supply at the gas temperature throughout, which requires slow expansion with good heat transfer. Real engine expansions are fast and nearly adiabatic, which is one reason they deliver less work than the isothermal ideal. The ratio of the two works here is 89.6/166.4 = 0.54.

Mistakes that cost marks. Using V₂ = 0.8 m³ for the adiabatic case (that is the isothermal end volume); writing W = mRT ln(V₂/V₁) without the mass and temperature, when p₁V₁ = 80 kJ is all that is needed; and saying “the adiabatic loses energy as heat”, when it exchanges no heat at all.
Closing check. Both satisfy Q − W = ΔU: 166.4 − 166.4 = 0 and 0 − 89.6 = −89.6 kJ.

bank.q: A rigid insulated tank is divided by a thin membrane. One side, 0.2 m³, holds air at 500 kPa and 300 K; the other side, 0.3 m³, is a vacuum. The membrane bursts. Using the first law, find the final temperature and pressure. Which part of your result holds for any gas, and which only for an ideal gas?
outline: System: all the gas in the whole tank; Q = 0 (insulated), W = 0 (rigid, expansion into vacuum)
First law: ΔU = 0 for any gas
Ideal gas: U depends on T only, so T₂ = T₁; then p₂ from pV = mRT
Real gas: U also depends on v, so T changes slightly
Irreversible: entropy rises and work potential is lost, which the first law does not show
answer: System. Take all the air as a closed system whose boundary is the inside of the tank wall. No mass crosses it.

Step 1: heat and work. The tank is insulated, so Q = 0. Its walls are rigid, and the air expands into a vacuum, pushing nothing (free expansion), so W = 0. The ∫p dV formula does not apply because the process is not quasi-static.

answer.pre: Q − W = ΔU   ⇒   0 − 0 = U₂ − U₁   ⇒   U₂ = U₁

answer: This holds for any gas, ideal or real: it uses only the energy balance.

answer.text: Step 3: ideal gas. For an ideal gas U = mcvT depends on T alone, so U₂ = U₁ gives

answer: Step 4: real gas. For a real gas U depends on temperature and specific volume. As the molecules move apart, work is done against their attractive forces, raising their potential energy; with U fixed, their kinetic energy, and so T, falls slightly. This Joule effect is very small for air near room temperature, which is why T₂ = T₁ is a good answer here, but it is a property of the gas, not a consequence of the first law.

head: Result
Holds for
rows: ideal gas only (needs T₂ = T₁ and pV = mRT)

answer: What the first law does not say. The process is irreversible: the gas never returns into one side by itself. Its entropy rises by mR ln(V₂/V₁) = 1.161 × 0.287 × ln 2.5 = 0.333 × 0.916 = 0.305 kJ/K. A slow, reversible isothermal expansion between the same end states would have delivered W = p₁V₁ ln(V₂/V₁) = 100 × 0.916 = 91.6 kJ of work (with 91.6 kJ of heat taken in). The free expansion wastes that chance, yet both satisfy the first law; only the second law shows the loss (see Limitations of the first law).

Mistakes that cost marks. Computing W = p₂(V₂ − V₁) or ∫p dV for the expansion (the gas pushes on nothing, so W = 0); taking the system as only the 0.2 m³ side, which then has mass leaving and needs an open-system balance; and writing “T₂ = T₁ for any gas”.
Closing check. p₂V₂ = 200 × 0.5 = 100 kJ = p₁V₁, as it must be at constant temperature for an ideal gas.

bank.q: State the limitations of the first law of thermodynamics. Use a paddle-wheel experiment and a hot cup of tea on a table to show what the first law does not tell us.
outline: The first law in one line and what it does decide
Limitations: direction, quality, PMM-2, equilibrium, reversibility
Paddle wheel: work → heat completely; the reverse never happens though it conserves energy
Tea: heat flows hot to cold; the reverse conserves energy too; entropy decides
Conclusion: the second law is needed
answer: What the first law does. It conserves energy: Q − W = ΔU for a process and ∮δQ = ∮δW for a cycle. It rejects any process that creates or destroys energy, such as a PMM-1. It is necessary, but it is a filter, not a full judge.

head: Limitation
What the first law cannot say
rows: whether a process that conserves energy will happen on its own, or only its reverse
that work is worth more than heat, or heat at 800 °C more than heat at 40 °C
that an engine turning all heat from one reservoir into work is impossible
whether a process wasted work potential, and how much

answer.text: Paddle wheel. A paddle stirs 2 kg of water in an insulated tank, doing 50 kJ of work on it. Q = 0, W = −50 kJ:

answer: All the work has become internal energy; the water warms by about 6 K. Now imagine the reverse: the water cools by 5.98 K and the paddle turns, delivering 50 kJ of work. Q − W = 0 − 50 = −50 kJ = ΔU, so the energy balance is perfect. It never happens. The first law cannot tell the two directions apart, and it hides the asymmetry behind them: work can turn completely into heat, but heat cannot turn completely into work in a cycle. That is the quality limitation.

answer.text: Hot tea. A cup holds 0.2 kg of tea (take c = 4.18 kJ/kg·K) at 80 °C in a room at 25 °C:
answer.pre: Q = mcΔT = 0.2 × 4.18 × 55 = 45.98 ≈ 46.0 kJ  (from the tea to the room)

answer: The reverse, 46.0 kJ flowing from the room back into the tea and re-heating it to 80 °C, balances energy just as well. Only the cooling happens. That is the direction limitation.

answer.text: What decides. The entropy of the isolated tea-and-room system:
answer.pre:
ΔS<sub>tea</sub>  = mc ln(T₂/T₁) = 0.836 × ln(298.15/353.15) = −0.1415 kJ/K
ΔS<sub>room</sub> = Q/T<sub>room</sub> = 45.98/298.15        = +0.1542 kJ/K
ΔS<sub>total</sub> = +0.0127 kJ/K > 0   (cooling is possible; re-heating would give −0.0127)

answer.text: Quality in numbers. The best any engine can do with heat at temperature T, rejecting to surroundings at 298 K, is to turn the fraction 1 − 298/T of it into work (the Carnot limit, from the second law):
answer.pre:
heat at 800 °C (1073 K):  1 − 298.15/1073.15 = 0.722  → at most 72 % can become work
heat at  40 °C (313 K):   1 − 298.15/313.15  = 0.048  → at most 5 % can become work

answer: To the first law both are simply kilojoules. This is the quality limitation in numbers, and it is why a power plant burns fuel at high temperature instead of using warm river water.

Evaluation. The two experiments show the same gap from two sides: energy is conserved in both directions, yet nature picks one. The second law fills the gap, in the Kelvin-Planck and Clausius statements and in the principle that the entropy of an isolated system never decreases. It also forbids the PMM-2, which the first law accepts, and through exergy it puts a number on the quality of energy. Neither law replaces the other: a process must pass both.
Closing check. 0.836 × 55 = 45.98 kJ and −0.1415 + 0.1542 = +0.0127 kJ/K, so the entropy test, not the energy test, separates the two directions of the tea example.

bank.q: Air at 0.2 kg/s flows steadily through a compressor, a cooler and a throttle in series. It enters the compressor at 100 kPa and 300 K and leaves at 500 kPa and 500 K with no heat loss; the cooler brings it to 310 K at 500 kPa; the throttle drops it to 100 kPa. Write the SFEE for each device, state which terms drop out and why, find the power and heat rates, and combine the three into one statement about the whole flow path (c<sub>p</sub> = 1.005 kJ/kg·K).
outline: Compressor: q = 0 here, ΔKE and ΔPE neglected: w = h₁ − h₂ (negative)
Cooler: w = 0: q = h₃ − h₂ (negative)
Throttle: q = 0, w = 0: h₄ = h₃; ideal gas so T₄ = T₃
Sum: q<sub>total</sub> − w<sub>total</sub> = h₄ − h₁
Comment on what the energy balance hides
answer: Assumptions for every device. Steady flow, ṁ = 0.2 kg/s through all three; uniform inlet and outlet properties; changes of kinetic and potential energy negligible (no velocities or heights are given and they are small beside the enthalpy changes); air an ideal gas, so h = cpT up to a constant.

answer.text: Compressor (1 → 2). No heat loss, so q = 0; work goes in.
Cooler (2 → 3). A heat exchanger: no shaft, so w = 0; pressure stays 500 kPa.
Throttle (3 → 4). No shaft and too fast for heat transfer: q = 0, w = 0.
answer.pre: h₄ = h₃   ⇒   T₄ = T₃ = 310 K   (ideal gas: h depends on T only)

answer: For real air near room temperature the Joule-Thomson effect would cool it by a few kelvin; the ideal-gas answer is the textbook one.

text-anchor="middle" style="fill:var(--ink)" font-weight="700">h₄ = h₃</text>

answer.text: Combined statement. Add the three SFEEs; the intermediate enthalpies h₂ and h₃ cancel:
answer.pre:
(h₁ − h₂ − w₁₂) + (h₂ − h₃ + q₂₃) + (h₃ − h₄) = 0
⇒ q<sub>total</sub> − w<sub>total</sub> = h₄ − h₁
numbers: −190.95 − (−201.0) = 10.05 kJ/kg = 1.005 × (310 − 300) ✓

answer: In words: for the whole path the shaft work put in minus the heat removed equals the rise in enthalpy of the stream from inlet to final outlet. Per second: 40.2 − 38.19 = 2.01 kW = ṁc<sub>p</sub>(T₄ − T₁) = 0.2 × 10.05.

Why each term drops out. In the compressor the question says no heat is lost; in a real machine q would be a small negative number and win = h₂ − h₁ − q. In the cooler nothing turns or moves a boundary, so w = 0; its pressure drop is neglected. In the throttle the flow is too fast for heat transfer and nothing turns, so q = w = 0; its exit velocity is assumed close to its inlet velocity, so the kinetic term cancels.

Energy bookkeeping in kW. Into the air: 40.2 kW of shaft power. Out of the air: 38.19 kW of heat to the cooling water. Kept by the air: 2.01 kW, carried away as a 10 K higher outlet temperature. Nothing is created or lost, which is all the first law can confirm.

What the balance hides. The air was compressed to 500 kPa at a cost of 40.2 kW, then throttled straight back to 100 kPa with no work recovered. The energy balance closes perfectly, yet the plant has thrown away the pressure it paid for. Only a second-law (exergy) analysis puts a number on that waste; this is a practical example of the limits of the first law.
Closing check. 201.0 − 190.95 = 10.05 kJ/kg, and 310 − 300 = 10 K × 1.005 = 10.05 kJ/kg: work in exceeds heat out by exactly the enthalpy the air keeps.

glossary.def: The quantity of matter or region of space chosen for study.
Everything outside the system boundary that can interact with the system.
A system of fixed mass; only heat and work cross its boundary. Also called a control mass.
A region fixed in space whose boundary mass may cross; used for open systems.
A quantity fixed by the state alone, such as pressure, temperature, U or H.
A quantity that depends on how a process is carried out; heat and work are path functions.
A series of processes that returns the system to its initial state.
Energy crossing a boundary because of a temperature difference.
Energy crossing a boundary by any means other than a temperature difference, such as a moving piston or a turning shaft.
E = U + KE + PE, the energy stored in a system.
The energy of the molecules of a system, excluding the motion and height of the system as a whole.
H = U + pV; per kilogram h = u + pv.
The work pv per kilogram done to push fluid across a boundary.
A process slow enough for the system to pass through equilibrium states, so that W = ∫p dV applies.
Expansion of a gas into a vacuum; no work is done and, for an ideal gas, the temperature does not change.
The heat needed to raise 1 kg of a substance by 1 K, at constant volume (c<sub>v</sub>) or constant pressure (c<sub>p</sub>).
R = R<sub>u</sub>/M, the constant in pV = mRT; 0.287 kJ/kg·K for air.
The exponent n in pV<sup>n</sup> = C.
A process with no heat transfer.
A process at constant temperature.
A process at constant pressure.
A process at constant volume.
A machine that would deliver work with no energy input, or more work than the heat supplied; forbidden by the first law.
A cyclic machine that would turn all heat from one reservoir into work; allowed by the first law, forbidden by the second.
Flow in which nothing inside the control volume changes with time.
A passage that speeds up a fluid at the expense of its enthalpy.
A passage that slows a fluid and raises its pressure and enthalpy.
Flow through a restriction with no heat or work transfer, so the enthalpy after equals the enthalpy before.
The model for filling and emptying vessels: uniform contents at each instant and fixed properties at each opening.
